extracted.intended_audience: general readers and bird enthusiasts interested in vulture species
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science/listicle article describing 18 vulture species with short profile entries including identification, range, behavior, and conservation notes. Each entry provides a quick-reference set of facts for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific name
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each species entry lists the binomial (e.g., Gypaetus barbatus). Placing the scientific name prominently under the common name helps with precise identification and cross-referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common name and grouping (Old World vs New World)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article separates species into Old World and New World vultures and lists common names (e.g., Bearded Vultures, Black Vultures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate whether a species belongs to Old World or New World groups and include the common name; use this grouping to highlight broad ecological/biogeographic differences (the page begins with two main groups and then enumerates species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range / distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of where the species is found (e.g., 'found in parts of southern Europe, central and southwestern Asia, the Indian subcontinent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide geographic range examples (countries, regions, continents). The article often notes country- or region-level distributions and isolated populations (e.g., isolated population in southwestern Europe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size metrics (wingspan, weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric size information such as wingspan and weight (e.g., 'wingspan can grow longer than 9 feet', 'weigh up to 30 pounds').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include typical wingspan and/or weight where known; comparative size claims (e.g., 'largest vultures', 'third largest Old World vulture') are used to add perspective and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet and feeding specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on diet (mostly carrion, bone marrow specialization, mammals, fish, reptiles, plant material) and feeding niche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe primary food sources and specializations (e.g., 'More than 90% of its diet consists of mammal carrion', 'bone marrow specialization'). Mention when species occasionally eat non-carrion items (garbage, plant material) or kill sick/dying animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding behaviors and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of how species obtain or access food (e.g., 'crack bones by dropping them from great heights', 'strongest bill… opening up carcasses first', bald head pushed into carcasses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List distinctive behaviours that affect feeding success: bone-cracking by dropping, biting through bones, relying on other species to open carcasses, keen sense of smell vs eyesight, bald head advantages, and order-of-access (which species open carcasses first).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social behavior and foraging dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the species is solitary, communal, forms flocks, nests in colonies, or forages/feeds together (e.g., 'very social, foraging and feeding together', 'solitary species – they’ll only congregate in groups when carrion is found').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate typical social structure (solitary, territorial pair, flocking, colony nesting) and how this affects detection of carrion and feeding. Note examples: griffon vultures nest in colonies on cliffs; white-headed vultures are solitary and territorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation status and threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit statements on conservation concerns and causes of decline (e.g., 'threatened species', 'population has declined from millions to less than 6,000', 'declining due to diclofenac poisoning', 'poaching, lead poisoning, habitat destruction').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize population trends and main threats; include specific anthropogenic threats when mentioned (veterinary drugs like diclofenac, habitat loss, fires, poaching, lead). Highlight species listed as endangered, vulnerable, or threatened where the article does so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification / distinctive physical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual ID details such as plumage color, head color, white lining under wings, ruffs, baldness, and color patterns (e.g., 'bald red head', 'white back on top of their brown wings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide key field marks useful for identification (head color, plumage contrasts, juvenile vs adult differences). The article uses these to help readers visually distinguish species in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat and nesting preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical habitats and nesting behavior (e.g., 'establish nesting colonies on cliffs', 'breed on cliffs', 'found near coast, foraging the area near the coast').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note preferred habitats (cliffs, coast, forests, open areas) and nesting/roosting sites. Include whether species are loyal to an area or migrate/roam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notable facts and life-history notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional notable data such as lifespan, breeding rate, sexual maturity, and unique records (e.g., 'live up to 40 years', 'only have one young per nest', 'unproven reports of 11-foot wingspans').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include life-history tidbits that inform rarity or conservation (low reproductive rate, late maturity) and interesting extremes or records that engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological role and summary context
rubrics_metrics.description: Summative statements of ecological importance and distinctions between groups (e.g., 'Vultures are crucial members… they clean up the remains of dead animals, thus preventing the development of diseases.'; 'These birds are separated into two groups Old World and New World vultures.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude species accounts with a 'big picture' summary: explain vultures' ecosystem services, summarize group-level comparisons (size, distribution), and reiterate conservation importance as the article's final thoughts do.
